paragraphs.heading: What makes a mammal
paragraphs.text: Mammals are backboned animals that form the class Mammalia, a name taken from the Latin word for breast. Four traits mark them out. Mothers feed their young with milk from mammary glands, the brain has a broad region called the neocortex, the body carries fur or hair, and the middle ear holds three bones. These features separate mammals from reptiles and birds, and the science that studies them is called mammalogy.

paragraphs.heading: Deep roots
paragraphs.text: The ancestors of mammals split away from the line leading to reptiles and birds in the Carboniferous period, more than 300 million years ago. Mammals are the only living members of a group called the synapsids. They arose from cynodonts, an advanced branch of the therapsids, somewhere between the Late Triassic and the Early Jurassic. Their modern variety came after the non-avian dinosaurs died out, and since 66 million years ago they have been the dominant animals on land.

paragraphs.heading: Many shapes and sizes
paragraphs.text: About 6,640 living species have been described, sorted into 27 orders. Rodents, bats and eulipotyphlans, such as hedgehogs, moles and shrews, have the most species, followed by primates, even-toed ungulates and the Carnivora. Most mammals get around on four limbs, but in some the limbs are adapted for life in the sea, in the air, in trees or underground. They range from the bumblebee bat, 30–40 millimetres long, to the 30 metre blue whale, possibly the biggest animal ever. Lifespans run from two years in the shrew to 211 years in the bowhead whale.

paragraphs.heading: Birth and young
paragraphs.text: Apart from the five monotreme species, which lay eggs, all modern mammals bear live young. The group richest in species is the placental mammals. They take their name from the placenta, a temporary organ through which the developing young draws nourishment from its mother during pregnancy.

paragraphs.heading: Minds and societies
paragraphs.text: Most mammals are intelligent, and some show large brains, self-awareness and the use of tools. They communicate in many ways, including ultrasound, scent marking, alarm signals, song, echolocation and, in humans, complex language. Their social lives vary widely, from fission–fusion societies, harems and hierarchies to animals that live alone and hold a territory. Most species are polygynous, but some are monogamous or polyandrous.

paragraphs.heading: Mammals and people
paragraphs.text: Taming mammals played a big part in the Neolithic Revolution, when farming took over from hunting and gathering as the main way people got food. That change moved human societies from wandering to settled life, with ever larger groups working together, and in the end led to the first civilizations. Domestic mammals still supply power for transport and farming, along with meat, dairy products, fur and leather. Many mammals are now declining or have gone extinct, driven mainly by poaching and habitat destruction, above all the cutting down of forests.
